summary: Lists the parameters used by ASAP and ENRP, the protocols in the Reliable Server Pooling architecture. It collects the values and registrations those protocols need, so they can be implemented consistently. It is published as an experimental document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5354 defines the shared data formats that ASAP and ENRP use in messages. It lists how parameters identify addresses, transports, pool members and errors, but leaves protocol procedures to other documents.

questions: what parameters do asap and enrp share
subtitle: Shared parameter formats used by the ASAP and ENRP protocols in Reliable Server Pooling.

tldr.problem: ASAP and ENRP use common message parameters. Different implementations need shared definitions for their types, values and error reports to interpret messages consistently.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies common Type-Length-Value parameter formats for addresses, transports, pool information, server identifiers and errors. It also defines the common message header and IANA registries.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5354 is Experimental. It specifies parameter formats only; protocol procedures are defined in the companion ASAP and ENRP RFCs.

today: RFC 5354 is Experimental. It specifies common parameter formats for ASAP and ENRP; it does not define their message procedures.

sections.title: The Common Parameter Specification
sections.content:
Aggregate Server Access Protocol (ASAP) and Endpoint Handlespace Redundancy Protocol (ENRP) are companion protocols in the Reliable Server Pooling architecture. They share parameters in their message formats.

This RFC defines those common parameter formats. It does not explain the procedures for composing or using ASAP and ENRP messages; the RFC points readers to the respective protocol specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: ASAP and ENRP need to agree on the structure of shared message data. This RFC specifies those formats, while companion RFCs explain how the protocols use them.

sections.title: Parameters and Message Layout
sections.content:
Each parameter uses a Type-Length-Value format. A 16-bit type identifies the parameter, and a 16-bit length gives its size. Parameter data is padded with zero bytes when needed so the total parameter length is a multiple of four bytes; the length field does not include this padding.

Common messages have an 8-bit message type, 8-bit flags, a 16-bit length and a variable message value. Messages also use four-byte alignment. All parameter values are transmitted in network byte order.
sections.plainLanguage: Each parameter starts with a type and length, followed by its data. Padding aligns it to a four-byte boundary, and the length excludes that padding.

sections.title: Addresses and Transport Parameters
sections.content:
Address parameters carry IPv4 or IPv6 addresses. Transport parameters describe DCCP, SCTP, TCP, UDP or UDP-Lite endpoints, including their port and address information. An SCTP parameter can contain more than one IP address; the other listed transport parameters contain one.

A pool element parameter carries information such as a pool-element identifier, registration lifetime, user transport, selection policy and ASAP transport. A server-information parameter describes an ENRP server and its transport address.
sections.plainLanguage: Transport parameters tell the protocols which address and port to use for a service. Pool and server parameters identify the members and ENRP servers that provide it.

sections.title: Errors, Registries and Security
sections.content:
An Operation Error parameter carries one or more error causes. The registered causes include an unknown parameter or message, invalid values, a non-unique pool-element identifier, a lack of resources, an unknown pool handle and a security-related rejection.

The RFC establishes IANA registries for RSerPool parameter types and error causes. Its Security Considerations section says these common formats add no security constraints; ASAP and ENRP security details are handled in their own specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: The error parameter identifies why a message could not be processed. This RFC defines the shared error formats but does not add security rules for either protocol.
